challenges.situation: A job candidate arrives at an interview wearing an expensive watch, casually mentions their Ivy League degree, and name-drops a famous former boss — all in the first two minutes. What information should you extract from this behavior?

options.text: Their status is uncertain and they're investing costly resources to establish it — which means they may or may not be as qualified as the signals suggest
options.feedback: Aggressive signaling tells you status is 'in play' — uncertain and needing proof. This is Bayesian evidence that updates in both directions: they might genuinely be accomplished (the signal is honest) or they might be stretching (the signal is inflation). It's not automatically positive (option B) or negative (option C). And it's definitely not irrelevant (option D) — signaling behavior IS information about status confidence.

options.text: They're clearly high-status and qualified since they can afford these signals
options.feedback: Not quite. Aggressive signaling tells you status is 'in play' — uncertain and needing proof. This is Bayesian evidence that updates in both directions: they might genuinely be accomplished (the signal is honest) or they might be stretching (the signal is inflation).

options.text: They're insecure and compensating — strong candidates don't need to signal
options.feedback: Not quite. Aggressive signaling tells you status is 'in play' — uncertain and needing proof. This is Bayesian evidence that updates in both directions: they might genuinely be accomplished (the signal is honest) or they might be stretching (the signal is inflation).

challenges.situation: Mark Zuckerberg wore a hoodie to Wall Street investor meetings in 2010. Analysts were scandalized, but his status only increased.
challenges.question: What force made this countersignal work?

options.text: Power — his status was so established (worth $10B) that NOT signaling communicated 'I don't need your approval,' which only the very powerful can afford
options.feedback: Countersignaling works through power: only someone whose position is unquestionable can afford to not play the signaling game. The room already knew Zuckerberg was worth billions — the hoodie said 'I'm beyond needing to impress you.' If an unknown 26-year-old did the same thing, it would read as incompetence, not power. The mechanism is power-based, not identity or trust.

options.text: Identity — the hoodie was authentic to his identity as a tech founder and signaled he wouldn't change for anyone
options.feedback: Not quite. Countersignaling works through power: only someone whose position is unquestionable can afford to not play the signaling game. The room already knew Zuckerberg was worth billions — the hoodie said 'I'm beyond needing to impress you.

options.text: Status — wearing informal clothes in a formal setting disrupted the hierarchy and put him on top
options.feedback: Not quite. Countersignaling works through power: only someone whose position is unquestionable can afford to not play the signaling game. The room already knew Zuckerberg was worth billions — the hoodie said 'I'm beyond needing to impress you.

options.text: Trust — by being informal he signaled trustworthiness and accessibility that suited executives lack
options.feedback: Not quite. Countersignaling works through power: only someone whose position is unquestionable can afford to not play the signaling game. The room already knew Zuckerberg was worth billions — the hoodie said 'I'm beyond needing to impress you.

challenges.back: A signal is honest BECAUSE it's costly — only genuinely fit organisms can survive despite the handicap. The peacock's tail proves fitness precisely because it's a burden.

challenges.instruction: Match each concept to its description:

pairs.left: MBA from a top school ($200k + 2 years)
pairs.right: Costly signal of discipline, class, and network — works because it's expensive to fake

pairs.left: CEO wearing sneakers to a formal board meeting
pairs.right: Countersignal — status so established that informality reads as confidence, not ignorance

pairs.left: Gazelle bouncing high in front of a predator
pairs.right: Honest signal: 'I'm so fit I can waste energy — don't bother chasing me'

pairs.left: Posting a photo from a first-class lounge once
pairs.right: Cheap/questionable signal — low cost reduces informational value (could be upgrade or one-time)

pairs.left: Billionaire moving to 'dark social' (no public presence)
pairs.right: Privacy as the new countersignal — absence from public platforms signals 'beyond needing attention'

challenges.context: Which response shows better understanding of the underlying dynamics?

scenarioA.label: Reading signals at face value
scenarioA.text: Impressive credentials and expensive displays mean someone is impressive. Casual appearance means someone isn't serious. I judge people by what they show me.

scenarioB.label: Reading the signal economics
scenarioB.text: I ask: what's the cost of this signal? Who can afford it? What audience is it designed for? Aggressive signaling means status is uncertain. Countersignaling means status is unquestionable. Both are data — but about confidence level, not actual quality.

challenges.explanation: The second response shows structural awareness — recognizing the game and changing it, rather than just playing harder within the existing frame.

principle.text: Signaling is spending resources to communicate qualities that can't be directly observed. It works because only those who genuinely possess the quality can afford the signal's cost.
principle.subtext: Countersignaling is NOT spending resources — which communicates that your status is so secure it doesn't require proof. It works only when the audience already knows your position.

reflection: Where are you signaling too hard — spending resources to prove something that secure people wouldn't need to prove?
